name: The Straw Man
statement: Beat a distorted, feeble version of your opponent's argument and pretend you've defeated the real one.
statementAccent: a distorted, feeble version of your opponent's argument
meaning: The straw man is an informal fallacy in which someone refutes an argument that was not actually advanced by their opponent, misrepresenting, exaggerating, oversimplifying, or fabricating the opponent's position so it is easier to attack, then knocking down that distorted version and claiming to have defeated the real argument. The name comes from the image of a straw man, a scarecrow or training dummy, that is trivially easy to knock down compared with a real opponent. By covertly replacing the genuine position with a weaker one, the arguer wins only an illusory victory over a distortion the other side never held. One of the most common and recognised fallacies in debate, politics, and rhetoric, it is a failure of honest argumentation whose antidote is engaging the strongest version of an opponent's case.
mechanism: The fallacy works by substitution: the arguer quietly swaps the opponent's actual claim for a distorted proxy that is easier to attack, refutes the proxy, and presents this as refuting the original. The distortion can take several forms: quoting out of context, exaggerating a claim to an absurd extreme, picking a weak or fringe version of a position and treating it as the whole, or inventing a position no one holds. Because the audience may not notice the swap, the demolition of the straw man looks like a genuine rebuttal. The honest counter-move is steelmanning, applying the principle of charity by addressing the strongest, most defensible form of the opponent's argument rather than the weakest, so that any victory is over the real position.

examples.text: Responding to a call for moderate regulation by attacking the idea of banning everything distorts the position into an extreme no one proposed.
Selecting the most extreme, unrepresentative statement from a few members of a group and treating it as the whole group's position is a straw-man variant.
The remedy is to steelman, engaging the strongest version of the opponent's argument through the principle of charity rather than a weak caricature.

variants.name: The hollow man
variants.text: A wholly fabricated position, attributed to no real opponent, invented purely so it can be knocked down.

variants.name: The weak man
variants.text: Attacking a genuine but unusually weak version of a position and treating it as representative of the whole, a softer cousin of the straw man.

whyItMatters: The straw man is one of the most pervasive and easily recognised fallacies in public argument, from political debate to online discussion, and spotting it is a basic skill of critical thinking. Because it manufactures the appearance of victory without engaging the real disagreement, it degrades the quality of debate, entrenches positions, and misleads audiences into thinking a case has been answered when it has not. Understanding it also points to a constructive practice, steelmanning, in which one deliberately confronts the strongest form of an opposing view.

working.lead: Compare the target to the original
working.text: check whether the argument being attacked is the one actually advanced or a distorted, weakened proxy of it.
look for quoting out of context, exaggeration to an extreme, or attacking a fringe version as if it were the whole position.
engage the strongest, most charitable version of the opponent's argument, so any refutation lands on the real position.

limits: The straw man is committed only when the opponent's position is distorted; refuting a genuinely weak argument that someone actually made is not a straw man but fair criticism. Distinguishing a distortion from a legitimate interpretation can be contestable, since arguments are sometimes genuinely unclear and a good-faith reading may differ from the arguer's intent. The precise origin of the term is unclear, with the man-of-straw idiom old and the named fallacy appearing in later logic texts, so it is a well-recognised pattern rather than a coinage with a single author. It names a failure of relevance and honesty, not a formal logical error, so identifying it requires judgement about what was really claimed.
misreadings: A straw man is a misrepresentation of the opponent's argument, distinct from attacking the person, which is an ad hominem; the two are different fallacies. Refuting a genuinely weak argument someone actually made is not a straw man, since the fallacy requires distorting, exaggerating, or fabricating the position rather than merely disagreeing with it. And it is not simply any strong rebuttal; the flaw lies specifically in the covert swap of the real claim for a feebler one, so a fair, accurate refutation, however forceful, is not a straw man.
origin: A classic informal fallacy of relevance whose precise origin is unclear; the man-of-straw idiom is old, related arguments were described by Isaac Watts in 1724, and it appears as a named fallacy in later logic texts.
